text: Aleksei Morozov / Age: 37
Rank/Position: Junior Sergeant, deputy squad leader
Civilian Occupation: Tractor driver (kolkhoz)
Origin: Kursk region, RSFSR
Aleksei Morozov was kept alive by hatred.
Not hatred for the Hungarians across the river, or the occasional German you could spot among them.
Those men were just obstacles.
Things standing between him and whatever counted as home now.
What pumped blood through his veins, day after day, moment after moment, was contempt.
Contempt for his uncle. For how he ruined his family.
Aleksei's father was a simple, hard-working man,
a man who spent his whole life farming and tending animals.
He didn't understand big politics, and he didn't want to.
He believed that anything he needed, he could produce with his own hands.
For a long time, it looked like the world would prove him right.
His patience and his discipline built a respectable fortune.
It even survived the chaos of the civil war years, somehow,
despite the state taking whatever it could from the countryside.
But his father never watched the horizon.
He watched only his fields.
So the burden of keeping up with the world fell onto Aleksei and his mother, Anna.
They were the ones who tried to warn him.
They told him collectivization was coming.
That it was inevitable. That they should sell what they could while they still could. The
equipment, the threshing machine, the livestock. Turn it into money. Then leave — fast. Cross
the border. Disappear.
Aleksei's father may have seen the logic in it, but the thought of leaving his country,
of the danger, the unknown, terrified him.
And that fear is probably why he listened to his younger brother, Pyotr.
Pyotr insisted better days would come.
There was no need to panic.
Don't sell.
Don't run.
Hide what you can.
Bury it.
Stash it away.
When the good times return, you'll still have something to reach for.
Aleksei's father trusted his brother. Why wouldn't he? He didn't even know that Pyotr had already
joined the Komsomol, that he was already building himself a future, that he had ambitions that needed
a ladder, and nothing built a ladder faster than discovering — and smoking out — a kulak.
So Pyotr wrote a speech.
And he delivered it at the town's first quarterly meeting of 1930. Aleksei wasn't
there, but others were. Men who would later become his friends. They told Aleksei
what they saw. They repeated the story so many times that Aleksei began to see it
too. He pictured the scene so vividly that he could
imagine the smallest twitch in his uncle's face as he betrayed his own brother. The armed
brigade came the next morning. They didn't leave until they had turned the house inside
out, until they had found everything on the list Pyotr had given them. What made it worse
was that Aleksei's family hadn't just kept their wealth. They had tried to hide it.
So they deported the whole family.
Party people moved into their home.
Pyotr was appointed brigade leader, and from that day on, a large letter marked Aleksei's
papers.
A “K.” It branded him, and it branded his son, born three years later.
The stigma followed the boy into school. It sat there in the class
register like a stain that wouldn't wash out. Aleksei's father couldn't carry the weight of the
betrayal. He hanged himself. His mother didn't last much longer. Grief and shame finished what the
state had started. Aleksei became a tractor driver. Year after year he planned revenge against his uncle,
and year after year he postponed it — for the sake of his family, for the sake of his son,
until the war arrived. The war that took so much from him that consequences stopped mattering.
Now, out here on this frozen no-man's-land, it is the promise of future retribution that
moves his limbs. It is faith — cold, clean
faith — that a day will come when he can take the rifle he holds right now, press the barrel
into his uncle's mouth, and squeeze the trigger. He imagines it with the calm of a man imagining
sunrise. Not because he loves killing.
Because he loves the idea of debt being paid.
